case.question: What caused the September 4 pool incident and what corrected it?
expected_points: rollback and move acquisition after inventory

chunk.title: Current configuration reference (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Current configuration reference (synthetic) | Historical comparison
The 2026-09-04 pool incident involved a historical per-process pool limit of 12. The current limit of 20 came from a separate capacity review. The incident correction was acquiring a connection after the inventory request, not a blanket recommendation to enlarge pools. Always compare the revision and process scope before treating historical configuration as current.

chunk.title: Pool checkout regression incident (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Pool checkout regression incident (synthetic) | Timeline
Historical synthetic incident on 2026-09-04, all times UTC. At 10:00 a release introduced growing DB_POOL_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT counts. At 10:08 traces showed a connection was checked out before an inventory-api call and held during slow inventory responses. At 10:17 operators rolled back the release. By 10:22 acquisition waits returned to the pre-incident range.

chunk.title: Pool checkout regression incident (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Pool checkout regression incident (synthetic) | Findings and scope
The affected revision used 12 connections per process. The confirmed finding for this historical incident was a code path holding database connections across inventory calls; it was not proof that PostgreSQL capacity was exhausted. The corrective change moved connection acquisition after the inventory operation and added a regression test. The current revision uses 20 connections after a separate capacity review; increasing the pool was not the documented incident fix. This historical finding does not diagnose a new event.

chunk.title: Inventory path latency incident (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Inventory path latency incident (synthetic) | Timeline
Historical synthetic incident on 2026-10-02, all times UTC. At 14:00 inventory request latency increased after a network routing change. At 14:06 dependency spans showed long connection-establishment time while database pool acquisition remained normal. The routing change was reverted at 14:12. By 14:20 inventory request durations returned to baseline.

case.question: Which fields correlate pool waits with inventory requests?
expected_points: acquisition time versus inventory elapsed time

chunk.title: Telemetry field guide (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Telemetry field guide (synthetic) | Correlation and pool fields
request_id identifies a caller request; trace_id connects its spans. Compare signals in the same time window and process. db_pool_in_use is the number of checked-out connections in one process; compare against 20 for the current revision. db_pool_waiters counts pending acquisitions. db_pool_acquire_ms measures time spent waiting for a slot; it is not SQL execution duration.

chunk.title: Database connection-pool exhaustion runbook (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Database connection-pool exhaustion runbook (synthetic) | Distinguishing checks
DB_POOL_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT means order-api waited 500 ms for a pool slot. Compare db_pool_in_use with the per-process limit of 20, db_pool_waiters, and db_pool_acquire_ms for the same process and time window. A full pool with waiting requests supports investigating pool contention; it does not prove that PostgreSQL itself is unavailable. The error differs from DEPENDENCY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT, which describes waiting for inventory-api rather than acquiring a database connection.

chunk.title: Inventory dependency timeout runbook (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Inventory dependency timeout runbook (synthetic) | Distinguishing checks
DEPENDENCY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT means the order-api inventory client exceeded its 1500 ms request deadline. Inspect dependency_name, upstream_status, inventory_request_ms and trace spans for the same request_id and time window. A missing upstream_status can mean no response was received before the deadline; it does not establish whether inventory-api completed the operation. Compare database pool metrics separately: DB_POOL_ACQUIRE_TIMEOUT indicates waiting for a database slot, not an inventory response.

chunk.title: Database connection-pool exhaustion runbook (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Database connection-pool exhaustion runbook (synthetic) | Follow-up evidence
Inspect active and long-running transaction durations, connection checkout duration and recent request concurrency. Correlate slow inventory calls with long checkouts to test whether a code path holds a connection while waiting on a dependency. The intended request path calls inventory-api before acquiring a database connection. A connection leak, long transaction, or burst of concurrency can produce similar symptoms; request traces and pool metrics are needed to distinguish them.

chunk.title: Telemetry field guide (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Telemetry field guide (synthetic) | Dependency fields
inventory_request_ms measures elapsed client time for an inventory request. dependency_name identifies the upstream. upstream_status is the received HTTP status when available; it may be absent on a timeout. Inspect connection-establishment and response-wait spans separately. The corpus documents field meanings but includes no current field values.

chunk.title: Inventory path latency incident (synthetic)
chunk.text:
Inventory path latency incident (synthetic) | Findings and scope
For this historical event, the investigation attributed the delays to the changed network route. The client deadline was 1500 ms. Operators correlated caller spans with the routing change before reverting it. No evidence in this report establishes the cause of today's timeout, and a timeout alone cannot identify network routing as the cause. No automatic stock-reservation retry was introduced.

Inventory path latency incident (synthetic) | Findings and scope
For this historical event, the investigation attributed the delays to the changed network route. The client deadline was 1500 ms. Operators correlated caller spans with the routing change before reverting it. No evidence in this report establishes the cause of today's timeout, and a timeout alone cannot identify network routing as the cause. No automatic stock-reservation retry was introduced.

The 2026-09-04 pool incident involved a historical per-process pool limit of 12. The current limit of 20 came from a separate capacity review. The incident correction was acquiring a connection after the inventory request, not a blanket recommendation to enlarge pools. Always compare the revision and process scope before treating historical configuration as current.

Inventory path latency incident (synthetic) | Timeline
Historical synthetic incident on 2026-10-02, all times UTC. At 14:00 inventory request latency increased after a network routing change. At 14:06 dependency spans showed long connection-establishment time while database pool acquisition remained normal. The routing change was reverted at 14:12. By 14:20 inventory request durations returned to baseline.

chunk.text:
Pool checkout regression incident (synthetic) | Findings and scope
The affected revision used 12 connections per process. The confirmed finding for this historical incident was a code path holding database connections across inventory calls; it was not proof that PostgreSQL capacity was exhausted. The corrective change moved connection acquisition after the inventory operation and added a regression test. The current revision uses 20 connections after a separate capacity review; increasing the pool was not the documented incident fix. This historical finding does not diagnose a new event.
